full_judgment:
By this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the pendente lite- transferee -petitioners question the propriety of the order dated August 2, 1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sathkhira in Title Suit No.4 of 1991 refusing to implead them as defendants in a Suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and also a declaration that kabala deeds dated 7-4-1942 and 23-2-1943 and Danpatra deeds dated 12-5-1977 are forged, collusive and are of no legal effect 

 2. A brief resume of the events leading to issuance of this Rule would be quite instructive in the matter. Opposite Party No. 1 is the plaintiff. He filed the suit as the reversioner of the owner of the properties under dispute in the suit. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 19 have been contesting the suit by presenting written statement. The petitioners by way of several kabala deeds dated July 19, 1993 purchased 20.42 acres of land from defendant Nos. 1, 2, 11, 13, 19, 20 and 21 during the pendency of the suit 

 3. The petitioners on 2-8-1993 filed an application in the Court under the provisions of Order 22, rule 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be impleaded as defendants in the suit raising the contentions that the transferor- defendants having extinguished their right, title, interest and possession over the suit land by way of different sale deeds in their favour, they are not interested to proceed further with the suit to protect their interest and, as such, they are needed to be impleaded as defendants in the suit. In the said application it is also averred that the petitioners were not at all aware of the institution of the Suit and petitioner No.6 only on 21-7-1993, for the first time, got knowledge of the said suit and on enquiry became confirmed of the said matter. 

 4. The learned Assistant Judge rejected the said application by the impugned order dated August 2, 1993 holding that the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 19 have been contesting the suit and the transfer made by them in favour of the petitioners is not valid and the contesting defendants without waiting for the final result of the suit transferred the suit land in favour of the petitioners and intentionally created an obstacle in the proper adjudication of the suit. In rejecting the said application the learned Judge took the view that the petitioners did not file the application with clean hands and mind. The learned judge, ultimately, found that the petitioners are not necessary parties for proper adjudication of the case. 

 5. Aggrieved by such adjudication by the learned Assistant Judge, the petitioners approached this Court in an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule raising the contention that the defendants by transferring the suit land to the petitioners lost their interest in the suit and the petitioners are the only interested parties in place of the transferor-defendants and the learned Assistant Judge failed to consider this legal aspect of the matter and committed a substantial error in not impleading the petitioners as defendants in the suit. 

 6. The plaintiff-opposite-party No. 1 entered appearance in the Rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit-in-opposition taking the stand that the petitioners being well aware of the institution of the suit by the plaintiff purchased the suit land and they are not proper parties for adjudication of the suit. Further stand taken is that the rights of the transferees, if any, are well protected under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. It is also stated that the alleged transfers are not, only pendente-lite but also made fraudulently at a very belated stage when the suit was at the peremptory stage. Further contention is that the learned Assistant Judge properly exercised his discretion in .passing the impugned order and no prejudice has been caused to the petitioners. 

 8. The learned Advocate for the Plaintiff-Opposite party at the very outset raised a preliminary objection that the application for impleading as parties was filed under the provisions of Order 22, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said application having been refused, appeal lies under the provision-of Order 43 rule 1(1) of the Code and the Revision preferred against the said' order under section 115(1) of the Code is not at all maintainable. 

 9. In repelling the said objection the learned Advocate for the petitioner advanced submission that though the application for addition of party was filed under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code but virtually that is an application under Order 1 rule 10(2) of the Code and the learned court also treated the application as one under Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code and Civil Revision under section 115(1) of the Code is quite maintainable. 

 10. In the wake of rival contentions advanced from both the sides, it is beneficial to extract both order 22, rule 10 and Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Order 22, Rule 10 reads thus: "10. (1) In other cases of an assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suit, the suit may, by leave of the Court, be continued by or against the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved; (2) The attachment of a decree pending an appeal therefrom shall be deemed to be an interest entitling the person who procured such attachment to the benefit to sub-rule (1)." Order 1 rule 10(2) runs thus: "10(2) the Court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such, terms as may appear to the Court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendants, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added." 

 12. From a reading of the provision of Order 22, rule 10 it is manifestly clear that under Order 22, rule 10, in the cases of an assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pendency of the suit, the suit may, by leave of the Court, be continued by or against the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved and such person may apply to be impleaded as a party provided he is virtually interested in the litigation. The bare reading of sub-rule 2 of rule 10 of Order 1 reveals that the court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the Court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added. In dealing and considering the application both under Order 22, rule 10 or Order 1, rule 10(2) the court has to exercise the discretion judicially and also in consonance with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. 

 13. On perusal of the application filed under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code it transpires that the said application was filed by the petitioners to be added as defendants in the suit for the protection of their right and interest over the suit land and, although, the application was filed under Order 22, rule 10, the same is virtually an application under Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code. The learned Assistant Judge also treated the said application as one under Order 1, Rule 10(2) of the Code. The language of the court is quoted hereunder অর্ডার ১ রুল ১০ এর দ্বিতীয় দরখাস্ত (যাহার দরখাস্তকারী মোক্তার মাসুম আবেদীন দিং) শুনিলাম।”Mokthar Masum Abedin and others are transferee-petitioners. Keeping in view of the statements and language in the said application, I am also of this view that the application, though, filed under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code but virtually the same was an application under Order, 1 rule 10(2) of the Code. Since the said application is an application under Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code, rejection of the said application refusing to implead the petitioners as defendants in the suit is a revisable order needed to be revised in Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code and, as such, the Civil Revision is- quite maintainable. Misdescription of a provision of law or misquotation of a particular section or Order or Rule in the heading cannot stand in the way of the said application being considered to be under the relevant law and there cannot be any ground to refuse to grant the proper relief or reliefs to which a litigant public under the law is entitled to have in his favour. The preliminary objection, thus, fails. 

 14. Before parting with this question I like to point out that even if the application for addition for party be treated as framed under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code then also, the Civil revision can be converted into a Miscellaneous appeal under Order 43, rule 1(l) of the Code. In the ends of justice the High Court Division has the power to treat an application of Revision as an appeal and vice versa a memorandum of appeal as an application for- Revision. 

 15. Now the single and sole question that survives for determination is, whether the petitioners can be impleaded as defendants in the suit. 

 16. Before I deal with this question it will be profitable to state the principle of law embodied in section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and the right of pendent lite purchaser to be joined as a party in a suit. Section 52 enacts the doctrine of Lis Pendens which is expressed in the maxim "ut pendente nihil innovetur."The doctrine is derived from the rules of jus gentium which becax embodied in the Roman Law where there is the maxim: Ram (sic) de qua controversia probibemur  (sic) in acrum dedicare" which means a thing concerning which there is a controversy is prohibited, during the suit, from being alienated. In the Corpus Juris Secundum Vol. LIV, Page 570 the definition is stated thus: "Lis pendens literally means a pending suit; and the doctrine of lis pendens has been defined as the jurisdiction, power, or control which a court acquires over property involved in a suit pending the continuance of the action, and until final judgment therein." 

 17. Section 52, thus, enjoins that during the pendency in any Court in Bangladesh any suit or  proceeding which is not collusive and in which any  right to immovable property is directly and  specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of  any other party thereto under any decree or order  which may be made therein, except under the  authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose. It is intended by this provision of law to protect the parties to the litigation against alienation by the opposite parties during the pendency of the litigation. But it is well recognised that the effect of section 52 of Transfer of Property Act is not to wipe out a sale pendente lite altogether but to subordinate it to the rights based on the decree or the order passed in the proceeding. The transferee pendente lite takes a the property subject to the result of the suit or proceeding. It is to be noticed that the right under the decree or order is sought to be protected by the doctrine of lis pendens. But if the proceeding cannot yield any result creating any right in favour of a party to the proceeding, the question of applying the doctrine does not arise. The Supreme Court of India in Nagubai Ammal and others vs. B Shama Rao and others, AIR i956 SC 593 ruled: "The effect of  section 52 is not to wipe out a sale pendente lite  altogether but to subordinate it to the rights based on  the decree in the suit". The Supreme Court of India also considered the effect of the words used in section 52 "so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein" and observed that "the transfer is good except to the extent that it might conflict with rights decreed under the decree or order. It. is in this view that transfers pendente lite have been held to be valid and operative as between the parties thereto". The Supreme Court of India again in the case of Sm Saila Bala Dassi vs. Sm Nirmala Sundari Dassi and another, AIR 1958 SC 394 observed that as a purchaser pendente lite a person will be bound by the proceeding taken by the parties in whose favour the decree is passed in execution of the decree and justice requires that such purchasers should be given an opportunity to protect his right. I am in respectful agreement with the principle of law enunciated by their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India. 

 18. Let me now turn to the question whether the petitioners are required to be impleaded as defendants in the suit. The provisions contained in Order 1 rule 10(2) of the Code had already been quoted above. Order 1 rule 10(2) of the Code empowers the court to implead any person as party who ought to have been joined whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit. The exercise of discretionary power on the question of addition of party under rule 10(2) of Order 1 of the Code is a judicial discretion which has to be exercised keeping in view of the fact and circumstances of each and every case. Judicial discretion means a discretion which is informed by tradition. methodised by analogy and disciplined by system It is to be remembered that for effectual and complete adjudication and settlement of all the questions involved in the suit, a third party whose presence, even if unnecessary but proper, should be allowed to be added as a party if applied for. It is also to be looked that in a suit relating to property, the person to be added as a party must have a direct interest in the subject matter of the litigation. 

 19. In the case of Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia vs. Additional Member, Board of Revenue, Bihar and another, AIR 1963 SC 786 it was held by the Supreme Court of India that it is within the discretionary power of the court to add or implead proper parties for completely settling all the questions that may be involved in the controversy either suo motu or on the application of a party to the suit or an application filed at the instance of such other party. Similar view has been also expressed by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Munshi Ram vs. Narsi Ram and another AIR 1983 SC 271. 

 21. Coming back to the case, on my hand, it appears that land involved in the suit is 20.17112 acres on which the plaintiff prays for declaration of title and out of that 20.17ih acres of-land plaintiff prays for confirmation of possession with respect to 13.58 acres of land. The petitioners appear to have purchased 20.42 acres of land out of total 84.58 acres of land described in schedule-Ka to the plaint by several sale deeds dated 19-7-1993 from the transferor-defendants. It further transpires from materials on record that the petitioners became aware of the institution of the suit on 21-7-1993, only two days after their purchase by sale deed and filed the application for addition of parties on 2-8-1993, that is, only after 14 days of their purchase. It, thus, appears that the petitioners acted with due diligence and promptness and it cannot be said that there had been want of due diligence and also that they are guilty of unreasonable delay in moving the court to be impleaded as defendants in the suit to protect their rights and interests. It further appears that the' plaintiff purchased more land than the suit land as described in schedule-Kha to the plaint 

 22. It is pertinent' to note here that the petitioners claim to have purchased the plaint schedule-Kha and Ga property by way of a good number of sale deeds and also Danpatra deeds. Since the petitioners purchased the properties during the pendency of the suit they will be subjected to the result of the suit. It is asserted in the petition for addition of party that as the transferor-defendants sold away the properties they are not taking any interest in the suit and for the said reason they prayed to be impleaded as defendants just to protect their rights and interests which they acquired by way of several deeds of transfer. It is worthy to note that since the petitioners claim their interest through the transferor-defendants they will not get better rights than the transferor-defendants. The apprehension in the minds of the petitioners that the transferor- defendants are not interested to proceed with the suit cannot be said to be without any foundation. Weighing the entire facts, circumstances and materials produced before this Court and in the light of the proposition of law emerging, from the authorities referred to above, the' petitioners are required to be impleaded as defendants in the suit just to protect their right and interests and to finally adjudicate the dispute between the parties and, also, to shorten the litigation and avoid multiplicity of proceedings. The learned Assistant Judge failed to consider the compelling circumstances leading to the filing of the application for addition of parties in the suit by the petitioners and thus fell into an error of law in refusing them to implead as transferor- defendants in the suit and by the error a failure of justice has been occasioned. 

 23. From the impugned order it appears that the suit reached to its peremptory stage and the evidence of PW I Niranjan Kumar Mondal had been recorded in Part The suit having reached to its peremptory stage and evidence of PW 1 having been recorded in part the suit must not be dragged to an indefinite period at the sweet will of the petitioners Necessary directions for the speedy disposal of the suit are given below. Before concluding I am inclined to observe that the plaintiff shall be at liberty to demonstrate that the transfer made by the transferor-defendants in favour of the petitioners are collusive. 

 25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute The order dated 2-8-1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Satkhira in Title Suit No.4 of 1991 refusing to add the petitioners as defendants in the suit is set aside. The petitioners are added as defendants in the suit. 

 26. The petitioners are directed to file written statement within 15(fifteen) days of the receipt of the order of this Court and they are allowed 15(fifteen) days more to take all steps including the steps embodied under section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 27. The learned Assistant Judge is directed to dispose of the suit within 3(three) months of the receipt of the order of this Court.
